messages.subject: how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
messages.subject_clean: how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
messages.body_plain:
hi all, I've seen several related posts but so far none that answer my question.

We have made three visits over the course of several weeks to each of 30 point count stations, where we performed an 8-minute count on each visit.

We have imported all of the data into Distance, accounting for the three repeat visits as "survey effort" at the "point transect" level. So for each point, we have the name of the point, and the survey effort = 3. Then at the sample level, we have each observation with its distance, as well as covariates relating to the time and weather of each visit, and the visit number (1-3).

My question is: where in the modeling phase (the "inputs") do we bring the survey effort in? i.e., where do we tell Distance that we have repeated counts at each station, as opposed to all of those observations coming from a single visit.

I understand that the point may be moot because we have equal numbers of visits at all stations....but even if so, for the future, when that is likely to not be the case, I'd like to know how to model survey effort.

Thanks!
Cali

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
messages.body_plain:
Cali

Not sure I understand your question.  Sounds like you've set up your project properly.  You have recorded number of visits in the "Survey effort" field of the transect layer along with covariates (including visit number) at the observation layer.

Distance calculates encounter rate as the number of detections per unit of effort (visit).  Consequently by specifying 3 visits to the point, Distance calculates the proper encounter rate.  There is no need for the number of visits to be equal for all points.  Perhaps on one visit, you were unable to get to some of the points, therefore the number of detections on those points will be a function of 2 visits rather than 3; you merely indicate "Survey effort" of 2 for those points.

Your analysis will not model survey effort (it is known and not estimated), but the number of detections is a function of effort; that is taken into account in the manner I described.

messages.subject: Pooling data in Distance 6.2
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm a student in Perth, Western Australia studying arboreal possums and was hoping someone could help me figure out how to analyse the data correctly in Distance 6.2.
I have collected data from 4 consecutive nights/surveys (on the same transect) of spotlighting for possums, totalling 62 observations (22 on night 1, 13 on nights 2 and 3 and 14 on night 4).
I'm led to believe with a low number of observations I can pool the data from all nights to get a better detection function and pdf but I don't know how to go about it.
I have set the data up so the stratum/region is listed as 1 for all observations, the area is the same for all (420ha), but I have made each night of spotlighting data a different number under the line transect heading (ie 1,2,3 and 4), followed by the transect length and perpendicular distance. Is this correct?
I have also run the analysis with all observations as number 1 under the line transect heading, which gives a higher density estimate, but this seems statistically invalid.
Is it possible to pool the data and use the detection function or probability density function from the pooled data for each nights data seperately?
Or am I way off track? unfortunately my supervisors have little to no experience with this program
Any help is appreciated
Regards
Adrian Barrett

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Pooling data in Distance 6.2
messages.body_plain:
Adrian:

Given you have walked but a single transect, you will not really be able to make inference to a "study area" as you lack replicates to assess how encounter rates change across your study area.

When transects are walked multiple times during a survey, the usual way to enter this into Distance is to multiply the length of the transects by the number of times they are walked.  This will adjust the pooled number of detections by the total amount of effort expended.

Therefore I would structure the project with a single region (as you have) and a single transect (length equal to 4X the transect length).  The analysis you perform will then use detection information from all nights to create your detection function.  Distance will also issue a warning, stating it cannot estimate encounter rate variance because you have but a single transect (as I noted in my first paragraph).  Therefore your inference will be limited to the area covered by your survey effort in the single transect.

messages.subject: I'm lost and I need help!
messages.subject_clean: I'm lost and I need help!
messages.body_plain:
Hi, everyone,

            I’ve been volunteering with USFWS to conduct shrub-steppe songbird point counts for the past few years. This year, I made the mistake of volunteering to try and analyze the data for them, as they are understaffed and underpayed.  DISTANCE was the recommened tool.  I may have bitten off more than I can chew, but I’m trying to figure this out.  But I can’t get the data I have to match what Distance is asking for….I’m a birder, not a biologist or statistician.

So, to summarize: in order to monitor shrub-steppe songbirds, avian point counts have been performed on the Fitzner-Eberhard Arid Lands Ecology Reserve (ALE), now part of the Hanford Reach National Monument according to the same protocol since 1997.  The only analysis performed to date analyzed data from 1997-2007 using repeated-measures mixed-effects models (Earnst et al 2009).  33 points were each sampled once per year, between May 1 and May 31.  The data collected records each bird sighted, and assigns it to a distance class of <50m, >50m, or as a “flyover”.  I would like to re-examine this data using the distance data to get a population density estimate for each species of concern for each year.  I would then attempt to correlate this to precipitation over previous winter, and to wildfire occurrence.

            So what I want is a number for D-hat for each species of interest for each year.  A quick glance over the data suggest that a given year results in about 500 sightings of about 30 species; half of the species are generally represented by a single individual, so I’ll ignore those.

            Bibby and Burgess (2000) suggests that getting the estimates I want using distance classes of 0 to 50m and 50m to infinity is possible, but I’m forced to assume a half-normal model for the detection curve.  That’s okay.  But what I don’t get is how to match up the data I have in hand to Distance 6.2’s data hierarchy.  “Observation,” obviously, is each individual sighting of a bird, with the distance.  “Sample” is going to be the individual point.  But where I’m stuck is defining the “Stratum” and “Global” layers.  Do I need to do each year as separate project?  Do I need to break it down to one species in one year equals one project?  If I do that, can I just get rid of the “stratum” layer?

            Other factors that could apply once I have this figured out is the time of day each sample was made, and also, observations are classified by time since the count started (0-3min, 3-5min, 5-10min) this means that I could start truncating the data, to get  a range for D-hat, as more time means more observations made.  But that can wait until I have a better understanding of the program.

            So for now, can anyone point me to what I need to do to get the data into Distance to get a basic density per species per year?  I realize that I’m asking a lot, but even some examples of similar projects or specific references to the User’s Guide or anything would be a help.  I’m trying to work it out, but I feel stuck.  I watched several YouTube videos by Eric Rexstad, but I’m still lost.  Thanks for anything you folks can provide.

Chad,  from Richland, WA, USA

References:

Bibby, C. and Burgess, N.  2000.  Bird Census Tecchniques, Second Edition.  Academic Press.

Earnst, S. L., Newsome, H. L., Laframboise, W. L., & Laframboise, N. (2009). Avian response to wildfire in interior columbia basin shrubsteppe. The Condor, 111(2), 370-376. doi:http://dx.doi.org/10.1525/cond.2009.080109

messages.body_plain:
Chad

Congratulations for volunteering your services.  Your question has quite a few facets a) data structure, b) detection function models and c) "other factors".

Regarding the mechanical aspects of getting your data into a format that Distance can analyse, I suggest you have a look at the sample projects that ship with the software.  There are three projects that you should examine (in increasing order of relevance):
 - amakihi.  Hawaii songbird study with 41 stations and 7 seasonal visits; there were 3 covariates considered in modelling the detection function.
 - housewren.  This has 10 plots, each with multiple points.  The points have multiple visits with data collected by multiple observers.  It is a songbird riparian habitat survey in Colorado, described in Section 8.6 of Buckland et al. (2001).
 - "songbird"  This was a study of multiple species in 4 pastures over 2 years (pasture x year considered strata).  This study is described in Section 8.7 of Buckland et al. (2001).

Examining these projects you will see the "global" layer is the study area, with "region" constituting strata for which you wish to have estimates.  In your situation, you might consider years as strata, similar to the "songbird" project.

Regarding your second point, regarding fitting detection functions to these data, you are correct that you might be able to fit a half-normal detection function (without adjustments) to the data collected according to the protocol you describe.  However there are two challenges to this.  First, animal movement causes bias in density estimates, particularly for point counts where observers are stationary; that suggests the "flyover" category should be excluded from your analysis.  Second, having but two distance categories considerably limits your modelling abilities.  Without exact distance measurements to the detections, you cannot use such things as Kolomogorov-Smirnov goodness of fit tests (described in Burnham et al. (2004), Chapter 11 of Advanced Distance Sampling, and available in Distance).  Instead you are left with chi-square goodness of fit tests, described in Section 3.4.4 of Buckland et al (2001).  With 2 distance categories, there are no degrees of freedom with which to assess the fit of your 1-parameter half-normal model (2 categories - 1 model parameter - 1 = 0 df for goodness of fit test).  That is a challenge, because you are left to make inference from a model, whose fit cannot be numerically assessed.

Your last point about other information to incorporate into modelling, as you say, can wait until you grapple with items a) and b).

messages.subject: Help with survey design
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm planning to use Distance Sampling to estimate the population of and endangered songbird species. The forty-spotted pardalote (Pardalotus quadragintus) is endemic to Tasmania, Australia and I want to estimate the population in the North portion of an offshore island which is a stronghold for the species. The species is closely related to a tree species, the white gum (Eucalyptus viminalis) and it only occur in areas where this tree can be found. I have a shapefile from the Tasmanian vegetation with polygons of areas where white gums occur and I was wondering how can I use this to design a survey. Another thing is that the area is highly fragmented, it is embedded in a matrix of pastureland.

Since the species is dependent on the presence of white gums, my survey points would be deployed only in this polygons, right?
Also now is the breeding season for this species, would that be a problem?

Many thanks,

Fernanda Alves.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Help with survey design
messages.body_plain:
Fernanda

We don't necessarily have all the information needed to help you design your survey, but you have given us a few ideas.

I categorise your statement 'only occurs in areas where .. [white gum].. can be found' as an assumption.  To check the veracity of that assumption, you might consider allocating some survey effort outside the white gum patches; perhaps creating a stratum for pastureland habitat and a stratum for gum habitat.  Besides you need to travel from one patch to another somehow, perhaps you could collect data while in transit.  If the 'matrix' in which the white gum patches exist receive survey effort, then your inference can be made to the island (or whatever portion of the island receives sampling effort), rather than your inference restricted only to white gum patches.

If the white gum patch sizes are similar in size to the area of your point transects (I assume you will be using point transects), you may have 'edge effects'.  This situation is depicted in the figure below where circles are point transects, solid line is patch edge and dotted line is a buffer extending around the patch of width w=maximum detection distance. This figure is taken from Section 7.2.2.1 of the advanced distance sampling book by Buckland et al. (2004).

Finally, regarding the breeding season, I suspect this is a good time of year to detect vocalising males, but females are unlikely to be vocalising and most likely to be on the nest.  Hence, you will get an estimate for the male segment of the population and may need to assume for each male there is an undetected female; or merely make inference to the male segment of the population.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

First of all thank you for the answer. I'm just starting to think about the survey and actually now that I have more information I think I can explain better what I want. The habitat here is new for me and while looking at shapefiles of the region and talking to people that know more about the vegetation I think I can explain better. The pastureland is definitely not used by pardalotes, and I think that my strata would actually be remnants where white gums are know to be present in representative numbers and where they are not.

Forty spotted pardalotes are known to inhabit eucalyptus forest where white gums are present in large numbers because they provide a major source of food and this has been reported for many years (but yes this is an assumption). I have a shapefile with polygons (see figure attached) of areas where white gums are more common. However white gums can also occur sparsely in the rest of the landscape.

So my question is, when I plan my survey should I use these polygons to create strata and put random survey points in the polygons and in the rest of the forest remnants, creating in this way two strata. Actually another researcher has random survey points (200 m apart in the figure attached) established along this polygons for other survey purpose, so I was wondering if I could use his survey points within the polygons and establish new random survey points in the rest of the area.
Also can I put more survey effort in areas known to be potential habitat (polygons).

Another thing, even though we know that pardalotes don't use pastureland, I'd still have to survey this areas to be able to infer a population estimate for the north part of the Island? Because I thought that my study area would be based on the landscape that is covered by forest remnants.

​

 Many thanks,

Fernanda.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Help with survey design
messages.body_plain:
Fernanda

I take a pretty strict view on the subject of inference based upon sampling; others may take a more relaxed view.  If you design your survey in such a way there is no possibility of sampling habitat X, then you should not make inference about what might be occurring in habitat X.  In effect, you have placed habitat X outside your study area by excluding from receiving survey effort.

messages.body_plain:
Stuart

After the Rugby World Cup quarter-final match, I'm not sure those of us in Scotland are allowed to offer advice to someone of an Aussie persuasion.

Nevertheless, there is a discussion of the contents of the bootstrap file in the Distance Users Guide in the Appendix, MCDS Engine Reference, under the heading "Output from the MCDS Engine"

Rather than label the columns, this output file defines rows, and each row contains an identifier to indicate the information presented on that row.  Part of the table from the users guide that describes how the rows are labelled is here:

The ten columns of each row contain these 10 pieces of information (again a table from the users guide):

The bootstrap file will contain ~25 records for each bootstrap replicate.  Those records capture everything about that particular replicate, the likelihood value, the parameter estimates and uncertainties for all the detection function parameters, estimates of abundance (perhaps by strata), etc.

Here is a simple example.  The following 24 records from the bootstrap file are for the first replicate of a very simple (ducknest) dataset.

Using the tables above, the first record is

stratum 0
sample 0
estimator 1
module 1
statistic 1
namely, what is reported relates to the "encounter rate" module, the number of observations statistic (534) with no uncertainty

record 2 contains same as above, but now statistic 2 in the encounter rate module, namely number of samples (1)

skipping a few records,

stratum 0 sample 0 estimator 1 module 2 deals with detection probabilities
statistic 4 is the value of f(0)= 0.1441573 (that does have an SE, lower and upper CI bounds and associated df; filling out that record)
statistic 5 is probability of detection (P_a=0.8671082) with its measures of precision

skipping some more records

stratum 0 sample 0 estimator 0 module 4 deals with estimates of density or abundance
statistic 1 is density of clusters=127.0170 with associated precision
statistic 2 is density of animals=127.0170 (same, because nests were all singles)

So you can work through this bootstrap file to extract all of the replicate estimates of anything that is being calculated by Distance.

That will get you started, let us know if you have more questions.
